legacy_report:
SOURCE: "DeepSeek-OCR: Contexts Optical Compression", Haoran Wei, Yaofeng Sun, Yukun Li (DeepSeek-AI). It is arXiv:2510.18234v1 [cs.CV], dated 21 Oct 2025. The text calls itself a "technical report" and gives no venue, so treat it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: I read all 53,164 chars. That is the abstract, the body, Tables 1-4, the discussion and conclusion, and the start of the references. I skimmed the rest of the references, which hold nothing beyond citations. There are no appendices. I did not run the figure-caption script. Figure captions come from the extracted text, and the figure images were not viewed.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- Claim: Decoding precision stays high while text tokens are within about 10x the vision tokens, and falls off beyond that.
  number: 97% at <10x; about 60% at about 20x
  setup: Fox benchmark, English documents only, 100 pages with 600-1300 text tokens (tokenized with DeepSeek-OCR's own ~129k vocab). Tested only in Tiny (64 vision tokens) and Small (100) modes. Prompt "Free OCR." (no layout).
  quote: "when the number of text tokens is within 10 times that of vision tokens (i.e., a compression ratio < 10×), the model can achieve decoding (OCR) precision of 97%. Even at a compression ratio of 20×, the OCR accuracy still remains at about 60%."
  where: Abstract, p.1

- Claim: Per-bucket compression vs precision table (Table 2). Fox English, with the number of pages in each bucket.
  number: see rows below
  setup: as above. Compression = ground-truth text tokens / vision tokens. Small pages counts (4-28 per bucket).
  quote (verbatim rows, "text tokens: 64-vis precision/compression, 100-vis precision/compression, pages"):
  - "600-700 96.5% 10.5× 98.5% 6.7×7"
  - "700-800 93.8% 11.8× 97.3% 7.5×28"
  - "800-900 83.8% 13.2× 96.8% 8.5×28"
  - "900-1000 85.9% 15.1× 96.8% 9.7×14"
  - "1000-1100 79.3% 16.5× 91.5% 10.6×11"
  - "1100-1200 76.4% 17.7× 89.8% 11.3×8"
  - "1200-1300 59.1% 19.7× 87.1% 12.6×4"
  where: Table 2, p.10. The Figure 1(a) text gives 85.8% and 76.3% for two cells where the table says 85.9% and 76.4%.

- Claim: Headline intro numbers for compression bands.
  number: 96%+ at 9-10x, ~90% at 10-12x, ~60% at 20x
  quote: "Our method achieves 96%+ OCR decoding precision at 9-10× text compression,∼90% at 10-12× compression, and∼60% at 20× compression on Fox [21] benchmarks"
  where: Introduction, p.3. The authors add that accuracy is "being even higher when accounting for formatting differences".

- Claim: On real document parsing (OmniDocBench), 100 vision tokens beats GOT-OCR2.0 at 256 tokens, and under 800 tokens beats MinerU2.0 at about 7,000.
  number: Edit distance, English overall: Small (100 tokens) 0.221 vs GOT-OCR2.0 (256 tokens) 0.287. Gundam (795 tokens) 0.127 vs MinerU2.0 (6790 tokens) 0.133.
  setup: OmniDocBench, edit distance (lower is better). Token counts are the average vision tokens per page. For Base and Large, "valid" tokens after padding are in parentheses.
  quote: "Requiring only 100 vision tokens (640×640 resolution), DeepSeek-OCR surpasses GOT-OCR2.0 [38] which uses 256 tokens" and "Using fewer than 800 tokens (Gundam mode), DeepSeek-OCR outperforms MinerU2.0 [34] which needs nearly 7,000 vision tokens."
  where: Section 4.2, p.12

- Claim: Table 3 DeepSeek-OCR modes (English overall / Chinese overall edit distance).
  number: Tiny 64: 0.386/0.361. Small 100: 0.221/0.284. Base 256(182): 0.137/0.24. Large 400(285): 0.138/0.208. Gundam 795: 0.127/0.181. Gundam-M 200dpi 1853: 0.123/0.157.
  quote: "Base 256(182) 0.137 0.054 0.267 0.163 0.064 0.24 0.205 0.474 0.1 0.181" and "Gundam 795 0.127 0.043 0.269 0.134 0.062 0.181 0.097 0.432 0.089 0.103"
  where: Table 3, p.11. Competitors for context: dots.ocr 200dpi uses 5545 tokens and scores 0.125 (English). Pipeline tools such as MinerU-2.1.1 score 0.162. Gemini2.5-Pro scores 0.148. GPT4o scores 0.233.

- Claim: The vision tokens needed depend on document type. Slides need about 64 tokens, books and reports need about 100. Newspapers need Gundam modes.
  number: Newspaper edit distance: Tiny 0.94, Large 0.353, Gundam 0.122, Gundam-M 0.099. Slides: Tiny 0.116.
  setup: OmniDocBench categories (Table 4). Authors attribute this to text length: "text tokens in newspapers are 4-5,000".
  quote: "For newspapers, Gundam or even Gundam-master mode is required to achieve acceptable edit distances, because the text tokens in newspapers are 4-5,000, far exceeding the 10× compression of other modes."
  where: Section 4.2 and Table 4, p.12. One oddity in Table 4: FinancialReport scores 0.289 in Gundam but 0.034 in Gundam-M and 0.022 in Large.

- Claim: Production throughput for generating LLM/VLM training data.
  number: 200k+ pages/day on a single A100-40G; 33M pages/day on 20 nodes (8 A100-40G each)
  quote: "DeepSeek-OCR can generate training data for LLMs/VLMs at a scale of 200k+ pages per day (a single A100-40G)." and "DeepSeek-OCR can generate 33 million pages of data per day for LLMs or VLMs using 20 nodes (each with 8 A100-40G GPUs)."
  where: Abstract and Introduction. The paper gives no hardware or batch setup for these throughput figures.

- Claim: Architecture and mode settings.
  number: DeepEncoder is about 380M parameters. The decoder is 3B MoE with about 570M active. The compressor is 16x.
  setup: 80M SAM-base (window attention) feeds a 2-layer conv 16x token compressor, then 300M CLIP-large (global attention). Decoder: DeepSeek-3B-MoE, 6 of 64 routed experts plus 2 shared.
  quote: "a 1024×1024 image ... 1024/16×1024/16=4096 patch tokens ... the token count becomes 4096/16=256"
  where: Section 3.2.1, p.5
  Modes (Table 1):
  - Tiny 512 px, 64 tokens.
  - Small 640 px, 100 tokens.
  - Base 1024 px, 256 tokens.
  - Large 1280 px, 400 tokens.
  - Gundam: n×100+256 tokens, with n tiles from 2 to 9.
  - Gundam-M: n×256+400.
  - Valid-token formula (Eq. 1): N_valid = ⌈N_actual × [1 − (max(w,h) − min(w,h))/max(w,h)]⌉.

- Claim: Training data mix.
  number: 30M PDF pages in about 100 languages (25M Chinese and English, 5M other). Fine annotations: 2M pages each for Chinese and English. Plus 10M charts, 5M chemical formulas, 1M geometry samples. Overall mix is 70% OCR, 20% general vision, 10% text-only.
  setup: Sequence length 8192. Trained on 20 nodes × 8 A100-40G, global batch 640. Table 3 lists Tiny to Large and Gundam as trained together. Gundam-M comes from continued training on 6M samples.
  quote: "OCR data accounts for 70%, general vision data accounts for 20%, and text-only data accounts for 10%."
  where: Sections 3.4-3.5, pp.7-10

- Claim: The model does "deep parsing" with a prompt. Charts become HTML tables, chemical formulas become SMILES, simple geometry is supported, and natural images get dense captions. It also supports layout-aware markdown output.
  number: none
  setup: qualitative figures only (Figures 7-10), no metrics.
  quote: "<image>\n<|grounding|>Convert the document to markdown." and "<image>\nParse the figure."
  where: Section 4.3.1, pp.12-16

- Claim (speculative, not tested): Optical compression could serve as an LLM memory-forgetting mechanism. Older chat history would be rendered as images and progressively downsized.
  number: "10× compression efficiency" for dialogue histories beyond k rounds
  quote: "implementing optical processing for dialogue histories beyond 𝑘 rounds in multi-turn conversations to achieve 10×compression efficiency."
  where: Section 5, p.18, Figure 13

LIMITS
- The compression study is OCR reconstruction only, on 100 English Fox pages. Bucket sizes are as small as 4 pages, and there is no confidence interval.
- The authors concede it does not validate real context compression: "OCR alone is insufficient to fully validate true context optical compression". They list digital-optical interleaved pretraining and needle-in-a-haystack tests as future work.
- The Fox output format does not match the ground truth, so measured precision is probably understated. The paper gives no figure for the gap.
- Above 10x, precision falls. The authors give two possible reasons, more complex layout and blurring at 512 or 640 px. They propose no test to tell them apart.
- The Discussion says: "we acknowledge this is early-stage work".
- The model has no SFT stage, so it is not a chatbot and some abilities need completion prompts.
- Geometry parsing is described as "extremely challenging and has a long way to go".
- Table 3 compares against other systems at different DPI settings and token counts. The throughput claims come with no setup.
- The paper has no RAG, retrieval or chunking evaluation. It is parsing and OCR only.
- It is dated Oct 2025. Newer OCR and parsing models may have passed these results, so I cannot say from this source.

BUILDS ON (as credited)
- Vary (Wei et al.; ref 36): the SAM + conv compressor design and the DeepEncoder training recipe.
- SAM (Kirillov 2023) and CLIP (ref 29): the two encoder halves.
- DeepSeekMoE (refs 19, 20): the decoder.
- GOT-OCR2.0 (ref 38): the OCR 2.0 task framing and the training-data flywheel.
- InternVL2.0 (Chen 2024): the tiling method.
- NaViT / Patch n' Pack (Dehghani 2023): adaptive-resolution encoder comparison.
- Fox benchmark (ref 21) and OmniDocBench (ref 27): the evaluation sets.
- Nougat (Blecher 2023), MinerU (ref 34), PP-DocLayout (ref 33) and PaddleOCR (ref 9): used for annotation and as baselines.
- OneChart (Chen 2024) and Slow Perception (ref 39): chart and geometry data.
- OPT-IML (Iyer 2022; ref 15): the compact language model used in encoder pretraining.

CODE: none in the paper. The prompts are the useful pieces, quoted verbatim:
- "<image>\nFree OCR." (Section 4.1, no layout)
- "<image>\n<|grounding|>Convert the document to markdown." (Fig 7)
- "<image>\nParse the figure." (Fig 7)
The weights and code are at http://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR.

FIGURES (not rendered or viewed, captions from the extraction)
- Fig 1, p.1: (a) compression vs precision on Fox, (b) OmniDocBench edit distance against average vision tokens. It shows the headline trade-off at a glance.
- Fig 3, p.5: architecture (SAM, 16x conv, CLIP, 3B-MoE).
- Fig 4 and Table 1: resolution modes.
- Fig 5: layout-interleaved annotation format.
- Fig 13: the forgetting-curve analogy, mapping Gundam, Large, Base, Small and Tiny to older memory.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Table 2 extraction runs columns together, for example "6.7×7" is 6.7x compression with 7 pages. Table 3 has similar run-on cells, for example "Tiny640.386" is 64 tokens, 0.386, and "dots.ocr†200dpi" row values are fused. Re-check these against the PDF layout before quoting.
- Internal inconsistencies: Table 2 gives 85.9% and 76.4% where Figure 1(a) gives 85.8% and 76.3%. The abstract says "200k+ pages per day (a single A100-40G)", while the intro gives 33M pages per day on 20 nodes (160 GPUs), and the two do not obviously reconcile.
- Table 4 labels the last row "Guandam-M", a typo in the paper.
- The extracted text is saved at /tmp/deepseek_ocr.txt.
